title: The mathematics of neural networks
summary: Vectors, matrices, derivatives, backprop, softmax, probability, eigenvalues, optimizers and initialisation in NumPy.

lessons.title: Vectors and norms
lessons.body:
# Vectors and norms

To a neural network, everything is a vector: a list of numbers. An image is its pixels, a word is its embedding, and a layer's output is one number per unit. NumPy stores a vector as a one-dimensional array, and arithmetic works element by element.

The length of a vector is its norm. The usual one, the L2 norm, is the square root of the sum of squares, Pythagoras in any number of dimensions. The L1 norm adds absolute values instead. The distance between two vectors is the norm of their difference.

```python
import numpy as np

v = np.array([3.0, 4.0])
print(np.sqrt(np.sum(v ** 2)))  # 5.0
print(np.sum(np.abs(v)))        # 7.0
print(np.linalg.norm(v))        # 5.0
print(v / np.linalg.norm(v))    # [0.6 0.8]
```

Dividing a vector by its norm gives a unit vector: same direction, length 1. Models normalise vectors this way before comparing directions. The zero vector has no direction, so it cannot be normalised.
lessons.task: Write `l2_norm(v)` returning the L2 norm of a list or array as a float, without `np.linalg.norm`. Write `normalize(v)` returning a NumPy array of length 1 in the same direction, raising `ValueError` for the zero vector, and `distance(a, b)` returning the L2 distance between two vectors.

checks.name: the L2 norm
checks.code:
got = l2_norm([3, 4])
assert abs(got - 5.0) < 1e-12, got
got = l2_norm([1, 2, 2])
assert abs(got - 3.0) < 1e-12, got
assert isinstance(l2_norm([1.0]), float), type(l2_norm([1.0]))

checks.name: a unit vector
checks.code:
import numpy as np
got = normalize([0, 3, 4])
assert np.allclose(got, [0, 0.6, 0.8]), got
got = normalize(np.array([2.0, -2.0, 1.0]))
assert abs(np.sqrt(np.sum(got ** 2)) - 1) < 1e-12, got

checks.name: the zero vector
distance
checks.code:
got = distance([1, 1], [4, 5])
assert abs(got - 5.0) < 1e-12, got
got = distance([2, 2], [2, 2])
assert got == 0.0, got

hints: Square each element, add them up, take the square root.
`np.sqrt(np.sum(v ** 2))` after `v = np.asarray(v, dtype=float)`; wrap it in `float(...)`.
In `normalize`, compute the length first and `raise ValueError(...)` when it is 0, then return `v / length`.
lessons.explanation:
Adding absolute values gives the L1 norm, which is a real norm but a different one: for `[3, 4]` it says 7, not 5, so the vector it divides by does not come out with length 1. When a lesson or a paper says the norm without a qualifier, it means L2.

Dividing by zero in NumPy does not raise: it warns and fills the result with `nan`, which then spreads silently through every later calculation. Checking for the zero vector and raising is how you keep a bad input from turning into a page of `nan` far away from its cause.

lessons.title: Dot products and projections
lessons.body:
# Dot products and projections

The dot product multiplies two vectors element by element and adds the results: `a @ b`. It is the most common operation in a neural network, because every unit of a layer computes one dot product of its weights with its input.

Geometrically, `a @ b` equals `|a| |b| cos(angle)`. Dividing by both lengths leaves the cosine: 1 for the same direction, 0 for perpendicular vectors, -1 for opposite ones. Embedding search ranks results by this cosine similarity.

```python
import numpy as np

a = np.array([2.0, 1.0])
b = np.array([1.0, 0.0])
print(a @ b)  # 2.0
cos = a @ b / (np.linalg.norm(a)
               * np.linalg.norm(b))
print(round(cos, 3))  # 0.894
p = (a @ b) / (b @ b) * b
print(p, a - p)  # [2. 0.] [0. 1.]
```

The projection of `a` onto `b` is the part of `a` that points along `b`: `(a @ b) / (b @ b)` times `b`. What is left, `a` minus the projection, is perpendicular to `b`.
lessons.task: Write `cosine(a, b)` returning the cosine similarity as a float, `project(a, b)` returning the projection of `a` onto `b` as an array, and `orthogonal_part(a, b)` returning `a` minus that projection.

checks.name: cosine similarity
checks.code:
got = cosine([1, 0], [0, 3])
assert abs(got) < 1e-12, got
got = cosine([1, 2], [2, 4])
assert abs(got - 1) < 1e-12, got
got = cosine([1, 1], [-1, -1])
assert abs(got + 1) < 1e-12, got

checks.name: projection onto a long vector
checks.code:
import numpy as np
got = project([2, 1], [3, 0])
assert np.allclose(got, [2, 0]), got
got = project([1, 1, 0], [0, 0, 5])
assert np.allclose(got, [0, 0, 0]), got

checks.name: the rest is perpendicular
checks.code:
import numpy as np
a, b = np.array([3.0, -1.0, 2.0]), np.array([1.0, 2.0, 2.0])
rest = orthogonal_part(a, b)
assert abs(rest @ b) < 1e-12, rest @ b
assert np.allclose(rest + project(a, b), a), rest

checks.name: projecting twice changes nothing
checks.code:
import numpy as np
a, b = np.array([4.0, 1.0]), np.array([2.0, 2.0])
once = project(a, b)
twice = project(once, b)
assert np.allclose(once, twice), (once, twice)

hints: The projection's length along `b` is `(a @ b) / |b|`, and the direction is `b / |b|`.
Multiply those together and the two `|b|` factors become `b @ b`.
`return (a @ b) / (b @ b) * b`.
lessons.explanation:
Dividing by `|b|` once gives the right answer only when `b` already has length 1. The scalar `(a @ b) / |b|` is the length of the projection; to turn it into a vector you multiply by the unit vector `b / |b|`, which divides by `|b|` a second time. With `b = [3, 0]` the starter's projection is three times too long.

Two properties make a projection easy to test: what remains is perpendicular to `b`, and projecting a second time changes nothing. Checking such properties, rather than one hand-computed answer, catches mistakes in any direction.

lessons.title: Matrices as maps
lessons.body:
# Matrices as maps

A matrix `W` with `m` rows and `n` columns turns a vector of size `n` into one of size `m`: each output is the dot product of one row with the input. A dense layer is exactly this, plus a bias vector `b` of size `m`: `W @ x + b`.

```python
import numpy as np

W = np.array([[1.0, 0.0, 2.0],
              [0.0, 1.0, -1.0]])
b = np.array([0.5, 0.0])
x = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0])
print(W.shape, x.shape)  # (2, 3) (3,)
print(W @ x + b)  # [ 7.5 -1. ]
```

Shapes are the first thing to check. The columns of `W` must match the input, and its rows decide the output. Composing two layers multiplies their matrices: a `(4, 2)` matrix after a `(2, 3)` one maps 3 numbers to 4.

A layer from `n` inputs to `m` outputs has `m` times `n` weights and `m` biases. Counting parameters this way tells you how big a model is before you build it.
lessons.task: Write `layer(W, b, x)` returning `W @ x + b`, raising `ValueError` when `W`'s columns do not match the size of `x` or `b`'s size does not match `W`'s rows. Write `param_count(sizes)` returning the number of weights and biases in a stack of dense layers with those sizes, so `[3, 4, 2]` means 3 to 4 to 2.

checks.name: computes the layer
checks.code:
import numpy as np
W = np.array([[1.0, 2.0], [3.0, 4.0], [0.0, 1.0]])
got = layer(W, np.array([1.0, 0.0, -1.0]), np.array([1.0, 1.0]))
assert np.allclose(got, [4, 7, 0]), got

checks.name: rejects mismatched shapes
counts biases too
checks.code:
got = param_count([3, 4, 2])
assert got == 26, got
got = param_count([784, 128, 10])
assert got == 101770, got

checks.name: one layer and none
checks.code:
got = param_count([5, 1])
assert got == 6, got
got = param_count([7])
assert got == 0, got

hints: NumPy already refuses a wrong column count, but it happily broadcasts a bias of the wrong size in some cases. Check `W.shape` against both yourself.
Each layer from `n_in` to `n_out` has `n_in * n_out` weights and `n_out` biases.
`sum(n_in * n_out + n_out for n_in, n_out in zip(sizes, sizes[1:]))`.
lessons.explanation:
NumPy raises for `W @ x` with mismatched sizes, but adding a bias broadcasts: a bias of size 1, or a wrong-shaped one that happens to line up, slips through and produces numbers of the wrong meaning. A clear error naming both shapes, raised where the mistake happens, saves a long hunt later.

Forgetting the biases undercounts by one parameter per unit. For `784 -> 128 -> 10`, the classic digit classifier, that is 138 of 101,770, small here, but the habit of counting exactly matters when you estimate memory for a real model.

lessons.title: Batches of vectors
lessons.body:
# Batches of vectors

Networks process many examples at once. A batch is a matrix `X` of shape `(n, d)`: one row per example. To apply a layer to every row, multiply by the transpose: `X @ W.T + b`. The result has shape `(n, m)`, and `b` of shape `(m,)` is broadcast, added to every row.

```python
import numpy as np

X = np.array([[1.0, 0.0],
              [0.0, 1.0],
              [1.0, 1.0]])
W = np.array([[2.0, 0.0],
              [0.0, 3.0],
              [1.0, -1.0]])
b = np.array([0.0, 1.0, 0.0])
print(X @ W.T + b)  # shape (3, 3)
```

## Broadcasting pairs

Adding a size-1 axis lines arrays up for every pair: `A[:, None, :] - B[None, :, :]` has shape `(n, m, d)`, all differences between rows of `A` and rows of `B`. Summing the squares over the last axis gives every squared distance with no Python loop. Attention, nearest neighbours and clustering all start this way.
lessons.task: Write `batch_layer(X, W, b)` applying the layer `W @ x + b` to every row of `X`, returning shape `(n, m)`. Write `pairwise_sq_distances(A, B)` returning the `(n, m)` matrix whose entry `[i, j]` is the squared L2 distance between row `i` of `A` and row `j` of `B`, without Python loops.

checks.name: same as one row at a time
checks.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
X, W, b = rng.normal(size=(5, 3)), rng.normal(size=(4, 3)), rng.normal(size=4)
got = batch_layer(X, W, b)
assert got.shape == (5, 4), got.shape
want = np.array([W @ x + b for x in X])
assert np.allclose(got, want), got

checks.name: squared distances
checks.code:
import numpy as np
A = np.array([[0.0, 0.0], [1.0, 1.0]])
B = np.array([[3.0, 4.0], [1.0, 0.0], [0.0, 0.0]])
got = pairwise_sq_distances(A, B)
assert got.shape == (2, 3), got.shape
assert np.allclose(got, [[25, 1, 0], [13, 1, 2]]), got

checks.name: matches a loop
checks.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
A, B = rng.normal(size=(4, 5)), rng.normal(size=(6, 5))
got = pairwise_sq_distances(A, B)
want = np.array([[np.sum((a - c) ** 2) for c in B] for a in A])
assert np.allclose(got, want), got

hints: `W` has shape `(m, d)` and each row of `X` has size `d`; which side of `@` must `d` be on?
For distances, give `A` a new middle axis and `B` a new first axis, so their difference broadcasts to `(n, m, d)`.
`X @ W.T + b`, and `np.sum((A[:, None, :] - B[None, :, :]) ** 2, axis=-1)`.
lessons.explanation:
`X @ W` only works when `W` is square, and even then it computes the wrong thing: it multiplies by the transpose of the layer. With a non-square layer it fails on shapes, which is the kinder outcome. Writing the shapes next to each other, `(n, d) @ (d, m)`, shows which matrix needs the transpose.

`A - B` subtracts row `i` of `A` from row `i` of `B` only, and only when both have the same number of rows. The extra `None` axes are what pair every row with every other row; the price is an `(n, m, d)` array in memory, which is fine for batches but worth knowing for large ones.

lessons.title: Derivatives
lessons.body:
# Derivatives

The derivative of `f` at `x` is the slope of `f` there: how much the output changes per unit change of the input, for a very small change. Training a network is nothing more than following such slopes downhill.

You can estimate a derivative from two values of `f`. The forward difference `(f(x + h) - f(x)) / h` is the slope of a short line to the right. The central difference `(f(x + h) - f(x - h)) / (2 h)` looks both ways, and its error shrinks with `h` squared instead of `h`.

```python
def f(x):
    return x ** 3

x, h = 2.0, 1e-3
forward = (f(x + h) - f(x)) / h
central = (f(x + h) - f(x - h)) / (2 * h)
print(forward - 12)  # about 6e-3
print(central - 12)  # about 1e-6
```

Do not make `h` too small: below about `1e-8`, rounding in floating point swamps the difference. Around `1e-5` the central difference is accurate to many digits, which is why it is the standard way to test hand-written gradients.
lessons.task: Write `forward_difference(f, x, h=1e-5)` and `central_difference(f, x, h=1e-5)` returning the two estimates of the derivative of `f` at `x` as floats.

checks.name: slope of a line
checks.code:
got = central_difference(lambda x: 3 * x + 1, 5.0)
assert abs(got - 3) < 1e-6, got
got = forward_difference(lambda x: 3 * x + 1, 5.0)
assert abs(got - 3) < 1e-6, got

checks.name: forward is first-order
checks.code:
got = forward_difference(lambda x: x ** 3, 2.0, h=1e-3)
assert 5e-3 < got - 12 < 7e-3, got

checks.name: central is second-order
checks.code:
got = central_difference(lambda x: x ** 3, 2.0, h=1e-3)
assert abs(got - 12) < 2e-6, got

checks.name: works for any function
checks.code:
import math
got = central_difference(math.sin, 0.5)
assert abs(got - math.cos(0.5)) < 1e-9, got
got = central_difference(math.exp, 1.0)
assert abs(got - math.e) < 1e-8, got

hints: The central difference evaluates `f` on both sides of `x`.
The two points are `x + h` and `x - h`, so they are `2 * h` apart.
`return (f(x + h) - f(x - h)) / (2 * h)`.
lessons.explanation:
The forward difference is right on average but leans toward the side it looks at: for a curve, the error is about `h / 2` times the second derivative. With `h = 1e-3` and `x ** 3` at 2 that is about `6e-3`, far too much to tell a correct gradient from a slightly wrong one.

The central difference cancels that leaning term, because the curve bends the same amount on both sides. Its error falls with `h ** 2`, so the same `h` is a thousand times more accurate. It costs two calls of `f` per input, which is why it is a test for gradients, not a way to train.

lessons.title: The chain rule
lessons.body:
# The chain rule

A network is a chain of functions: a product, then an activation, then a loss. The chain rule says the derivative of a chain is the product of the derivatives of its links, each taken at the value that flowed into it.

For `L = (s - y) ** 2` with `s = sigmoid(z)` and `z = w * x`, the links are `dL/ds = 2 (s - y)`, `ds/dz = s (1 - s)` and `dz/dw = x`. Multiply them.

```python
import math

def sigmoid(z):
    return 1 / (1 + math.exp(-z))

w, x, y = 0.5, 2.0, 1.0
z = w * x
s = sigmoid(z)
dL_ds = 2 * (s - y)
ds_dz = s * (1 - s)
dz_dw = x
print(dL_ds * ds_dz * dz_dw)
```

Compute forward first and keep every intermediate value, then multiply the local derivatives on the way back. That order, forward then backward, is exactly what backpropagation does at scale.
lessons.task: Write `sigmoid(z)` and `loss_and_grad(w, x, y)` returning the pair `(L, dL_dw)` as floats for `L = (sigmoid(w * x) - y) ** 2`, using the chain rule.
lessons.solution:
import math


def sigmoid(z):
    return 1 / (1 + math.exp(-z))


def loss_and_grad(w, x, y):
    z = w * x
    s = sigmoid(z)
    loss = (s - y) ** 2
    dL_ds = 2 * (s - y)
    ds_dz = s * (1 - s)
    dz_dw = x
    return loss, dL_ds * ds_dz * dz_dw

checks.name: sigmoid
checks.code:
got = sigmoid(0)
assert abs(got - 0.5) < 1e-12, got
got = sigmoid(2) + sigmoid(-2)
assert abs(got - 1) < 1e-12, got

checks.name: the loss
checks.code:
import math
got, _ = loss_and_grad(0.5, 2.0, 1.0)
want = (1 / (1 + math.exp(-1)) - 1) ** 2
assert abs(got - want) < 1e-12, got

checks.name: matches a numerical derivative
checks.code:
for w, x, y in [(0.5, 2.0, 1.0), (-1.0, 0.3, 0.0), (2.0, -1.5, 1.0)]:
    h = 1e-5
    want = (loss_and_grad(w + h, x, y)[0] - loss_and_grad(w - h, x, y)[0]) / (2 * h)
    got = loss_and_grad(w, x, y)[1]
    assert abs(got - want) < 1e-7, (w, x, y, got, want)

hints: There are three links: the square, the sigmoid and the product `w * x`.
The sigmoid's derivative is `s * (1 - s)`, where `s` is its output.
lessons.explanation:
Skipping the middle link treats the sigmoid as if it passed changes through unchanged. It does not: near 0 it passes a quarter of a change, and far from 0 almost nothing. The starter's gradient points the right way but is several times too large, and it never shrinks when the sigmoid saturates.

Comparing with a central difference, as the third check does, is the routine way to catch a missing link. Every framework's autograd is the chain rule applied mechanically, and its developers test it exactly like this.

lessons.title: Gradients and gradient checking
lessons.body:
# Gradients and gradient checking

A loss depends on many parameters at once. Its gradient is the vector of partial derivatives, one per parameter: how the loss changes when only that one parameter moves. The gradient points uphill, the direction of steepest increase, so gradient descent steps against it.

A numerical gradient moves each coordinate in turn by `h` in both directions and takes the central difference. It costs two evaluations per parameter, far too slow for training, and exactly right for checking an analytic gradient on a small case.

```python
import numpy as np

def f(x):
    return x[0] ** 2 + 3 * x[0] * x[1]

x = np.array([1.0, 2.0])
grad = np.zeros_like(x)
for i in range(len(x)):
    e = np.zeros_like(x)
    e[i] = 1e-5
    grad[i] = (f(x + e) - f(x - e)) / 2e-5
print(grad)  # [8. 3.]
```

Compare the two gradients with a relative error, the size of their difference over the size of both. Below about `1e-7` they agree; above `1e-3` something is wrong.
lessons.task: Write `numerical_gradient(f, x, h=1e-5)` returning the central-difference gradient of `f` at the float array `x`, leaving `x` unchanged. Write `relative_error(a, b)` returning `|a - b| / max(|a| + |b|, 1e-12)` with L2 norms, as a float.

checks.name: gradient of a sum of squares
checks.code:
import numpy as np
x = np.array([1.0, -2.0, 0.5])
got = numerical_gradient(lambda v: np.sum(v ** 2), x)
assert np.allclose(got, 2 * x, atol=1e-6), got

checks.name: a cross term
checks.code:
import numpy as np
got = numerical_gradient(lambda v: v[0] ** 2 + 3 * v[0] * v[1], np.array([1.0, 2.0]))
assert np.allclose(got, [8, 3], atol=1e-6), got

checks.name: leaves x alone
checks.code:
import numpy as np
x = np.array([0.1, 0.2, 0.3])
before = x.copy()
numerical_gradient(lambda v: float(np.prod(v)), x)
assert np.array_equal(x, before), x

checks.name: relative error
checks.code:
got = relative_error([1.0, 0.0], [1.0, 0.0])
assert got == 0.0, got
got = relative_error([1.0, 0.0], [0.0, 1.0])
assert abs(got - 2 ** 0.5 / 2) < 1e-12, got
got = relative_error([0.0], [0.0])
assert got == 0.0, got

hints: Moving `x[i]` up by `h` and then down by `h` does not take you to `x - h`.
Build a fresh step vector for each coordinate and evaluate `f(x + step)` and `f(x - step)`, which leave `x` untouched.
`step = np.zeros_like(x); step[i] = h; grad[i] = (f(x + step) - f(x - step)) / (2 * h)`.
lessons.explanation:
The starter changes `x` in place: it adds `h`, then subtracts `h`, which is back at `x`, not at `x - h`. So it computes a forward difference, divided by `2 h`: half the gradient. Editing in place also risks leaving the caller's array changed by rounding, and that array is often the model's real weights.

Creating `x + step` builds a new array each time. That is slower, which does not matter for a check, and it makes the function safe to point at real parameters. The relative error is the right yardstick because gradients can be tiny or huge; an absolute tolerance would be too strict for one and too loose for the other.

lessons.title: Activations and their slopes
lessons.body:
# Activations and their slopes

Every activation has a simple derivative, best written in terms of its own output:

- sigmoid: `s (1 - s)`, at most 0.25, at `z = 0`
- tanh: `1 - t ** 2`, at most 1
- ReLU: 1 where the input is positive, 0 elsewhere

In a deep network, backpropagation multiplies one such slope per layer. Ten sigmoid layers multiply ten numbers no larger than 0.25, so the gradient reaching the first layer is at most `0.25 ** 10`, about one in a million. That is the vanishing gradient problem.

```python
import numpy as np

z = np.linspace(-4, 4, 5)
s = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))
t = np.tanh(z)
print(np.round(s * (1 - s), 3))
print(np.round(1 - t ** 2, 3))
print((z > 0).astype(float))
print(0.25 ** 10)
```

ReLU's slope is exactly 1 for active units, so it passes gradients through deep stacks unchanged. That, more than anything, is why it replaced the sigmoid in hidden layers.
lessons.task: Write `sigmoid_grad(z)`, `tanh_grad(z)` and `relu_grad(z)` returning the element-wise derivatives for a NumPy array `z` (ReLU's slope at exactly 0 is 0). Write `stacked_sigmoid_slope(z, depth)`: the derivative of the sigmoid applied `depth` times in a row, at `z`, as a float, by the chain rule.

checks.name: sigmoid and tanh slopes
checks.code:
import numpy as np
z = np.array([-1.0, 0.0, 2.0])
got = sigmoid_grad(z)
assert np.allclose(got[1], 0.25), got
got = tanh_grad(z)
want = (np.tanh(z + 1e-6) - np.tanh(z - 1e-6)) / 2e-6
assert np.allclose(got, want, atol=1e-8), got

checks.name: ReLU slope
checks.code:
import numpy as np
got = relu_grad(np.array([-2.0, 0.0, 3.0]))
assert np.array_equal(got, [0.0, 0.0, 1.0]), got

checks.name: a stack of sigmoids
the gradient vanishes
checks.code:
got = stacked_sigmoid_slope(0.0, 10)
assert got < 0.25 ** 10, got
assert got > 0, got

hints: Differentiate `tanh` with its own output: if `t = tanh(z)`, the slope is `1 - t ** 2`.
In the stack, each sigmoid sees the output of the previous one, not the original `z`.
Loop `depth` times: multiply `slope` by `sigmoid_grad(z)`, then set `z = sigmoid(z)`.
lessons.explanation:
Raising one slope to the power `depth` assumes every layer sees the same input. It does not: the second sigmoid sees `sigmoid(z)`, a number between 0 and 1, and its slope there is smaller. The chain rule takes each link's derivative at the value that actually reached it, which is why backpropagation must remember the forward pass.

For ReLU, the slope at exactly 0 is undefined; frameworks pick 0, and so should you, so that dead units stay dead in a consistent way. The tanh slope `1 - tanh(z)` is a typo with a real cost: it can go negative and flips the direction of learning.

lessons.title: Backpropagation by hand
lessons.body:
# Backpropagation by hand

A two-layer network: `h = tanh(W1 @ x + b1)`, then `out = w2 @ h + b2`, with loss `L = 0.5 (out - y) ** 2`. Backpropagation walks back through it, one link at a time, reusing what the forward pass stored.

```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
W1 = rng.normal(size=(3, 2))
b1 = np.zeros(3)
w2 = rng.normal(size=3)
x, y = np.array([1.0, -1.0]), 0.5
h = np.tanh(W1 @ x + b1)
out = w2 @ h
d_out = out - y          # dL/dout
d_w2 = d_out * h
d_h = d_out * w2
d_pre = d_h * (1 - h ** 2)
d_W1 = np.outer(d_pre, x)
print(d_W1.shape, d_w2.round(3))
```

Each gradient has the shape of its parameter. A weight matrix's gradient is the outer product of the gradient arriving at its output and the input it saw, `np.outer(d_pre, x)`. A bias's gradient is just the gradient arriving at its output.
lessons.task: Write `backward(params, x, y)` for the network above, where `params` is a dict with `W1`, `b1`, `w2` and `b2` (a float). Return the dict of gradients of `L` with the same keys and shapes (`b2`'s as a float). `forward(params, x)` is given.
lessons.starter:
import numpy as np


def forward(params, x):
    h = np.tanh(params["W1"] @ x + params["b1"])
    return params["w2"] @ h + params["b2"], h


def backward(params, x, y):
    out, h = forward(params, x)
    d_out = out - y
    d_h = d_out * params["w2"]
    return {
        "W1": np.outer(d_h, x),
        "b1": d_h,
        "w2": d_out * h,
        "b2": float(d_out),
    }
lessons.solution:
import numpy as np


def forward(params, x):
    h = np.tanh(params["W1"] @ x + params["b1"])
    return params["w2"] @ h + params["b2"], h


def backward(params, x, y):
    out, h = forward(params, x)
    d_out = out - y
    d_h = d_out * params["w2"]
    d_pre = d_h * (1 - h ** 2)
    return {
        "W1": np.outer(d_pre, x),
        "b1": d_pre,
        "w2": d_out * h,
        "b2": float(d_out),
    }

checks.name: matches numerical gradients
checks.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
params = {'W1': rng.normal(size=(3, 2)), 'b1': rng.normal(size=3), 'w2': rng.normal(size=3), 'b2': 0.2}
x, y = np.array([0.7, -1.2]), 0.4
got = backward(params, x, y)
def loss():
    return 0.5 * (forward(params, x)[0] - y) ** 2
for name in ['W1', 'b1', 'w2']:
    array = params[name]
    want = np.zeros_like(array)
    for i in np.ndindex(array.shape):
        old = array[i]
        array[i] = old + 1e-6
        up = loss()
        array[i] = old - 1e-6
        down = loss()
        array[i] = old
        want[i] = (up - down) / 2e-6
    assert np.allclose(got[name], want, atol=1e-6), (name, got[name], want)

hints: Between `d_h` and the first layer's parameters there is one more link: the tanh.
The tanh's local derivative is `1 - h ** 2`, using the stored output `h`.
`d_pre = d_h * (1 - h ** 2)`, then `W1`'s gradient is `np.outer(d_pre, x)` and `b1`'s is `d_pre`.
lessons.explanation:
The starter's output layer is right, so the gradients for `w2` and `b2` pass, but it sends the gradient straight from `h` into `W1` as if tanh were not there. The numerical check catches it at once. Skipping an activation's derivative is the most common mistake in hand-written backprop, and the second most common is using the input of the activation instead of its output.

The pattern generalises to any depth: keep every layer's output on the way forward, and on the way back multiply by each local derivative in turn. Autograd does exactly this bookkeeping for you, and knowing it lets you read shapes and debug gradients when something goes wrong.

lessons.title: Expectation, variance and likelihood
lessons.body:
# Expectation, variance and likelihood

A random variable takes values with given probabilities. Its expectation is the probability-weighted average of its values; its variance is the expected squared distance from that average. A sample mean from many draws approaches the expectation.

```python
import numpy as np

values = np.array([0.0, 1.0, 10.0])
probs = np.array([0.5, 0.4, 0.1])
mean = values @ probs
var = ((values - mean) ** 2) @ probs
print(mean, var)  # 1.4 8.44
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
draws = rng.choice(values, 10000, p=probs)
print(draws.mean().round(2))
```

## Likelihood

A model predicts a distribution, and training maximises the probability of the data it sees, the likelihood. In practice you minimise the negative log-likelihood. For a Gaussian with mean `mu` and spread `sigma`, it is `0.5 log(2 pi sigma ** 2) + (y - mu) ** 2 / (2 sigma ** 2)`. With `sigma` fixed, only the squared error depends on `mu`: mean squared error is Gaussian likelihood in disguise.
lessons.task: Write `expectation(values, probs)` and `variance(values, probs)`, raising `ValueError` when the probabilities are negative or do not sum to 1 (within `1e-9`). Write `gaussian_nll(y, mu, sigma)` returning the mean negative log-likelihood of the array `y` under a Gaussian, as a float.

checks.name: expectation and variance
checks.code:
got = expectation([0, 1, 10], [0.5, 0.4, 0.1])
assert abs(got - 1.4) < 1e-12, got
got = variance([0, 1, 10], [0.5, 0.4, 0.1])
assert abs(got - 8.44) < 1e-12, got
got = variance([3, 3], [0.2, 0.8])
assert abs(got) < 1e-12, got

checks.name: rejects bad probabilities
Gaussian negative log-likelihood
checks.code:
import math
got = gaussian_nll([0.0], 0.0, 1.0)
assert abs(got - 0.5 * math.log(2 * math.pi)) < 1e-12, got
got = gaussian_nll([1.0, 3.0], 2.0, 2.0)
want = 0.5 * math.log(8 * math.pi) + 1 / 8
assert abs(got - want) < 1e-12, got

checks.name: the sample mean is the best mu
checks.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
y = rng.normal(2.0, 0.5, size=200)
best = gaussian_nll(y, y.mean(), 0.5)
assert best < gaussian_nll(y, y.mean() + 0.05, 0.5), best
assert best < gaussian_nll(y, y.mean() - 0.05, 0.5), best

hints: Variance is the expectation of the squared distance from the mean, not of the squared value.
Check `np.any(probs < 0)` and `abs(probs.sum() - 1) > 1e-9` once, in a helper both functions use.
`mean = values @ probs; return float(((values - mean) ** 2) @ probs)`, and the NLL adds `0.5 * math.log(2 * math.pi * sigma ** 2)` to every term.
lessons.explanation:
The expected square `E[X ** 2]` is only the variance when the mean is 0. In general variance is `E[X ** 2] - E[X] ** 2`, or, more stably, the expected squared distance from the mean. Dropping the log term of the likelihood keeps the best `mu` the same but gives wrong values, and it matters as soon as `sigma` is learned too.

Seeing losses as negative log-likelihoods explains the common ones: squared error assumes Gaussian noise, and cross-entropy, in the next lesson, is the likelihood of a categorical distribution.

lessons.title: Softmax and cross-entropy
lessons.body:
# Softmax and cross-entropy

A classifier outputs one score per class, called logits. Softmax turns them into probabilities: exponentiate each, divide by the sum. Cross-entropy is the negative log of the probability given to the correct class.

Exponentials overflow: `exp(1000)` is infinite. Softmax does not change when you subtract the same number from every logit, so subtract the largest and the biggest exponent becomes `exp(0) = 1`. For the loss, use the log-sum-exp form: `-log p[t]` equals `logsumexp(z) - z[t]`, which never takes the log of a zero.

```python
import numpy as np

z = np.array([1000.0, 999.0, 0.0])
e = np.exp(z - z.max())
p = e / e.sum()
print(p.round(4))
lse = z.max() + np.log(e.sum())
print(lse - z[1])  # loss for class 1
```

The gradient of this loss with respect to the logits is the simplest in deep learning: `p` minus the one-hot vector of the target. It is large where the model is confidently wrong and 0 where it is perfectly right.
lessons.task: Write `softmax(z)` for a 1-D array, stable for large logits, `cross_entropy(z, target)` returning `-log softmax(z)[target]` as a float through log-sum-exp, and `cross_entropy_grad(z, target)` returning its gradient with respect to `z`.

checks.name: probabilities
checks.code:
import numpy as np
got = softmax(np.array([0.0, np.log(3.0)]))
assert np.allclose(got, [0.25, 0.75]), got

checks.name: large logits
checks.code:
import numpy as np, warnings
with warnings.catch_warnings():
    warnings.simplefilter('ignore')
    got = softmax(np.array([1000.0, 1000.0, 0.0]))
assert np.allclose(got, [0.5, 0.5, 0.0]), got

checks.name: cross-entropy
checks.code:
import math, numpy as np, warnings
got = cross_entropy(np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0]), 2)
assert abs(got - math.log(4)) < 1e-12, got
with warnings.catch_warnings():
    warnings.simplefilter('ignore')
    got = cross_entropy(np.array([0.0, 800.0]), 0)
assert abs(got - 800.0) < 1e-9, got

checks.name: gradient is p minus one-hot
checks.code:
import numpy as np
z = np.array([0.5, -1.0, 2.0])
got = cross_entropy_grad(z, 1)
want = np.zeros(3)
for i in range(3):
    e = np.zeros(3)
    e[i] = 1e-6
    want[i] = (cross_entropy(z + e, 1) - cross_entropy(z - e, 1)) / 2e-6
assert np.allclose(got, want, atol=1e-7), (got, want)
assert abs(got.sum()) < 1e-12, got.sum()

hints: `np.exp(1000)` is `inf`, and `inf / inf` is `nan`. Shift the logits first.
Subtract `z.max()` before exponentiating; for the loss, `logsumexp(z) = top + log(sum(exp(z - top)))`.
`return float(top + np.log(np.sum(np.exp(z - top))) - z[target])`.
lessons.explanation:
The direct formula is mathematically right and numerically broken: with logits in the hundreds, the exponentials overflow to infinity and softmax returns `nan`. Even after fixing softmax, `-log(p[target])` fails when `p[target]` rounds to 0, giving an infinite loss instead of 800.

Shifting by the maximum and working in log space costs nothing and removes both problems. That is why frameworks offer cross-entropy on logits, such as `nn.CrossEntropyLoss`, and why you should pass logits to it, not probabilities.

lessons.title: Eigenvectors and the SVD
lessons.body:
# Eigenvectors and the SVD

An eigenvector of a square matrix `A` is a direction that `A` only stretches: `A @ v = lam v`, with the eigenvalue `lam` the stretch. Multiply any vector by `A` over and over, normalising each time, and it turns toward the eigenvector with the largest eigenvalue. This is power iteration.

```python
import numpy as np

A = np.array([[2.0, 1.0], [1.0, 2.0]])
v = np.ones(2) + np.array([1.0, 0.0])
for _ in range(50):
    v = A @ v
    v = v / np.linalg.norm(v)
print(v.round(3), (v @ A @ v).round(3))
print(np.linalg.eigvalsh(A))  # [1. 3.]
```

## The singular value decomposition

Any matrix, square or not, factors as `U @ diag(S) @ Vt`, with orthonormal `U` and `Vt` and singular values `S` from largest to smallest. Keeping only the first `k` gives the best rank-`k` approximation, and the error left over is the root of the sum of the squared dropped singular values. Low-rank fine-tuning methods such as LoRA rely on weight updates being well approximated this way.
lessons.task: Write `power_iteration(A, steps=200)` for a symmetric matrix, starting from `np.ones`, returning `(value, vector)`: the largest eigenvalue as a float (as `v @ A @ v`) and its unit eigenvector. Write `low_rank(M, k)` returning the best rank-`k` approximation of `M`, using `np.linalg.svd(M, full_matrices=False)`.

checks.name: largest eigenvalue
checks.code:
import numpy as np
A = np.array([[4.0, 1.0, 0.0], [1.0, 3.0, 1.0], [0.0, 1.0, 2.0]])
value, vector = power_iteration(A)
want = np.linalg.eigvalsh(A)[-1]
assert abs(value - want) < 1e-8, (value, want)
assert abs(np.linalg.norm(vector) - 1) < 1e-12, vector
assert np.allclose(A @ vector, value * vector, atol=1e-6), vector

checks.name: low rank keeps the shape and the rank
checks.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
M = rng.normal(size=(6, 4))
got = low_rank(M, 2)
assert got.shape == (6, 4), got.shape
assert np.linalg.matrix_rank(got) == 2, np.linalg.matrix_rank(got)

checks.name: full rank gives M back
checks.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
M = rng.normal(size=(3, 5))
got = low_rank(M, 3)
assert np.allclose(got, M), got

checks.name: the error is the dropped singular values
checks.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
M = rng.normal(size=(5, 5))
S = np.linalg.svd(M, compute_uv=False)
got = np.linalg.norm(M - low_rank(M, 2))
want = np.sqrt(np.sum(S[2:] ** 2))
assert abs(got - want) < 1e-9, (got, want)

hints: `np.linalg.svd` returns the singular values as a 1-D array `S`, separate from `U` and `Vt`.
Each kept direction is scaled by its singular value: you need `diag(S[:k])` between the two factors.
lessons.explanation:
Leaving out `S` keeps the right directions but gives each one length 1, so the result has the right rank and the wrong size: it never reproduces `M`, even with every direction kept. The singular values carry all the scale; the factors `U` and `Vt` only rotate.

Power iteration is how many large-scale methods find the dominant direction without a full decomposition, using nothing but matrix-vector products. The SVD's error rule, the Eckart-Young theorem, is what makes low-rank compression predictable: you can read off, from the singular values alone, how much you lose by keeping `k` of them.

lessons.title: Learning rate and curvature
lessons.body:
# Learning rate and curvature

Near a minimum, a loss looks like a bowl: `f(x) = 0.5 x @ A @ x`, with `A` symmetric. Its gradient is `A @ x`, and the matrix `A`, the Hessian, holds the curvature. Its eigenvalues are the curvatures along its eigenvectors.

One gradient step is `x - lr A x`. Along an eigenvector with eigenvalue `lam`, that multiplies the coordinate by `1 - lr lam`. When `|1 - lr lam|` is below 1 the coordinate shrinks; above 1 it grows every step and training diverges. So the learning rate must stay below `2 / lam_max`.

```python
import numpy as np

A = np.diag([1.0, 20.0])
x0 = np.array([1.0, 1.0])
for lr in (0.05, 0.11):
    x = x0.copy()
    for _ in range(50):
        x = x - lr * (A @ x)
    print(lr, np.abs(x).round(4))
```

The steepest direction caps the step size, while the flattest decides how many steps you need. Their ratio, the condition number, is why some losses train slowly at any learning rate.
lessons.task: Write `max_stable_lr(A)` returning `2 / lam_max` for a symmetric matrix as a float (use `np.linalg.eigvalsh`). Write `converges(A, lr)` returning whether gradient descent on `0.5 x @ A @ x` shrinks every direction, and `descend(A, x0, lr, steps)` returning `x` after that many steps.

checks.name: the largest eigenvalue sets the limit
checks.code:
import numpy as np
got = max_stable_lr(np.diag([1.0, 20.0]))
assert abs(got - 0.1) < 1e-12, got
got = max_stable_lr(np.array([[2.0, 1.0], [1.0, 2.0]]))
assert abs(got - 2 / 3) < 1e-12, got

checks.name: converges or not
checks.code:
import numpy as np
A = np.diag([1.0, 20.0])
assert converges(A, 0.09), 'lr 0.09 should converge'
assert not converges(A, 0.11), 'lr 0.11 should diverge'
assert not converges(A, 0.0), 'lr 0 never shrinks anything'

checks.name: agrees with descent

hints: `np.linalg.eigvalsh` returns the eigenvalues in ascending order.
Every factor `1 - lr * lam` must have absolute value below 1, including for the smallest `lam`.
`max_stable_lr` uses `eigvalsh(A)[-1]`; `converges` returns `bool(np.all(np.abs(1 - lr * eigvalsh(A)) < 1))`.
lessons.explanation:
`eigvalsh` sorts ascending, so index 0 is the smallest curvature. Using it allows a learning rate twenty times too large for the steep direction, which then explodes. The limit always comes from the steepest direction.

A learning rate of 0, or any rate where a flat direction's factor is exactly 1, also fails to converge: nothing explodes, but nothing shrinks either. Thinking in eigenvalues explains learning-rate warmup, adaptive optimizers and normalisation layers: all of them are ways of living with very different curvatures in one model.

lessons.title: Momentum and Adam
lessons.body:
# Momentum and Adam

Plain gradient descent zigzags across a narrow valley: the steep direction caps the learning rate, and the flat one barely moves. Two improvements dominate in practice.

Momentum keeps a running velocity, `v = beta v + g`, and steps `x - lr v`. Consistent gradients add up and speed the flat direction; alternating ones cancel.

Adam keeps running averages of the gradient, `m`, and of its square, `s`, and steps by `lr m / (sqrt(s) + eps)`, so every coordinate moves about `lr` regardless of its scale. Both averages start at 0 and are too small at first, so Adam divides them by `1 - beta ** t` at step `t`, which is bias correction.

```python
import numpy as np

g = np.array([0.01, 100.0])
m = 0.1 * g
s = 0.001 * g ** 2
print(m / (np.sqrt(s) + 1e-8))
m_hat = m / (1 - 0.9)
s_hat = s / (1 - 0.999)
print(m_hat / (np.sqrt(s_hat) + 1e-8))
```

Without the correction the first steps are three times too large. With it, the first step moves every coordinate by `lr`, whatever its gradient.
lessons.task: Write `momentum_step(x, v, g, lr, beta=0.9)` returning the new `(x, v)`, and `adam_step(x, m, s, g, t, lr, b1=0.9, b2=0.999, eps=1e-8)` returning the new `(x, m, s)` with bias correction, where `t` counts steps from 1. Use NumPy arrays and do not change the arguments in place.
lessons.starter:
import numpy as np


def momentum_step(x, v, g, lr, beta=0.9):
    v = beta * v + g
    return x - lr * v, v


def adam_step(x, m, s, g, t, lr, b1=0.9, b2=0.999, eps=1e-8):
    m = b1 * m + (1 - b1) * g
    s = b2 * s + (1 - b2) * g ** 2
    return x - lr * m / (np.sqrt(s) + eps), m, s
lessons.solution:
import numpy as np


def momentum_step(x, v, g, lr, beta=0.9):
    v = beta * v + g
    return x - lr * v, v


def adam_step(x, m, s, g, t, lr, b1=0.9, b2=0.999, eps=1e-8):
    m = b1 * m + (1 - b1) * g
    s = b2 * s + (1 - b2) * g ** 2
    m_hat = m / (1 - b1 ** t)
    s_hat = s / (1 - b2 ** t)
    return x - lr * m_hat / (np.sqrt(s_hat) + eps), m, s

checks.name: one momentum step
checks.code:
import numpy as np
x, v = momentum_step(np.array([1.0, 1.0]), np.array([0.5, 0.0]), np.array([1.0, 2.0]), 0.1)
assert np.allclose(v, [1.45, 2.0]), v
assert np.allclose(x, [0.855, 0.8]), x

checks.name: Adam's first step is lr per coordinate
checks.code:
import numpy as np
z = np.zeros(3)
x, m, s = adam_step(np.zeros(3), z, z, np.array([0.001, -5.0, 300.0]), 1, 0.01)
assert np.allclose(x, [-0.01, 0.01, -0.01], atol=1e-6), x
assert np.allclose(m, [0.0001, -0.5, 30.0]), m

checks.name: Adam later steps
checks.code:
import numpy as np
x, m, s = np.array([1.0]), np.zeros(1), np.zeros(1)
for t in range(1, 4):
    x, m, s = adam_step(x, m, s, np.array([2.0]), t, 0.1)
assert np.allclose(x, [0.7], atol=1e-6), x

checks.name: both beat plain descent on a narrow valley
checks.code:
import numpy as np
A = np.diag([1.0, 50.0])
x0 = np.array([1.0, 1.0])
plain = x0.copy()
x, v = x0.copy(), np.zeros(2)
a, m, s = x0.copy(), np.zeros(2), np.zeros(2)
for t in range(1, 101):
    plain = plain - 0.02 * (A @ plain)
    x, v = momentum_step(x, v, A @ x, 0.02)
    a, m, s = adam_step(a, m, s, A @ a, t, 0.05)
f = lambda p: 0.5 * p @ A @ p
assert f(x) < f(plain) / 10, (f(x), f(plain))
assert f(a) < f(plain), (f(a), f(plain))

hints: At step 1, `m` is `0.1 * g` and `s` is `0.001 * g ** 2`: both far smaller than `g` and `g ** 2`.
Divide `m` by `1 - b1 ** t` and `s` by `1 - b2 ** t` before the step, but return the uncorrected `m` and `s`.
`m_hat = m / (1 - b1 ** t)`, `s_hat = s / (1 - b2 ** t)`, `x - lr * m_hat / (np.sqrt(s_hat) + eps)`.
lessons.explanation:
Without bias correction the first step is `lr * 0.1 / sqrt(0.001)`, about `3.16 lr`, in every coordinate. Early steps too large by a factor of three can push a fresh network into a bad region before the averages warm up. The corrected values are only used for the step; the running averages themselves stay uncorrected, or the correction would compound.

On the narrow valley, momentum lets the flat direction build speed while the steep one oscillates and damps out, and Adam rescales each coordinate so the curvature difference matters far less. AdamW, the usual choice for transformers, is Adam with weight decay applied directly to the weights rather than through the gradient.

lessons.title: Initialisation and variance
lessons.body:
# Initialisation and variance

The variance of a sum of independent terms is the sum of their variances. A unit computes `w @ x` over `n` inputs; if each weight has variance `v` and each input variance 1, the output has variance `n v`. Choose `v = 1 / n` and the signal keeps its size from layer to layer. Too small, and it shrinks to nothing after a few layers; too large, and it explodes.

ReLU zeroes half of its inputs, halving the second moment, so ReLU networks use `v = 2 / n`, which is He initialisation, standard deviation `sqrt(2 / n)`. Xavier initialisation, `sqrt(2 / (n_in + n_out))`, balances the forward and backward passes for tanh.

```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
x = rng.normal(size=(1000, 256))
for std in (0.01, np.sqrt(2 / 256)):
    h = x
    for _ in range(10):
        W = rng.normal(0, std, (256, 256))
        h = np.maximum(h @ W, 0)
    print(round(std, 3), h.std().round(4))
```

Frameworks pick these scales for you, but a custom layer or a very deep stack is where knowing them pays off.
lessons.task: Write `he_std(fan_in)` and `xavier_std(fan_in, fan_out)` as floats. Write `relu_stack_stds(x, width, depth, std_fn, seed)`: starting from the batch `x`, apply `depth` layers `h = relu(h @ W)` with `W` of shape `(h.shape[1], width)` drawn from `np.random.default_rng(seed)` normal with standard deviation `std_fn(fan_in)`, and return the list of each layer's pre-activation standard deviations (of `h @ W`).

hints: With `1 / n`, each ReLU layer halves the variance, so after 12 layers the signal is `2 ** -6` of its size in variance.
He initialisation doubles the variance to make up for the half that ReLU zeroes.
`he_std` returns `float(np.sqrt(2 / fan_in))`.
lessons.explanation:
`sqrt(1 / n)` is the right scale for a linear layer, or for tanh near 0, but ReLU throws away the negative half of every pre-activation. Each layer then loses half the second moment, and twelve layers shrink the standard deviation by a factor of 8. Gradients shrink the same way on the way back, so the early layers barely learn.

Variance arithmetic is enough to predict this before training anything. The same reasoning explains why residual connections scale their branches, and why normalisation layers, which reset the variance at every layer, made very deep networks trainable.
